99.title: Knees and bows
99.hook: the knee bends toward the tabernacle; the head bows at the name of Jesus
99.howItsDone: Catholics genuflect on the right knee toward the tabernacle when entering or leaving a pew, bow their heads at the name of Jesus, and bow at the words of the incarnation in the Creed; those who cannot kneel make a bow instead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, holy water at the door, and the baptism it recalls. Your line was every door a baptism. Which doorway did you pause at? Day ninety-nine.

Before a Catholic slides into a pew, something odd happens. They stop in the aisle, face the front, and drop down on one knee. Just for a second, then up again, and in they go. If you didn't grow up with it, it can look like someone about to propose, or tie a shoe. Then, later in the Mass, you'll see a whole church bow their heads at the same moment, like wheat in the wind. Nobody announced it. Everyone just knew. Camp Three is about the body praying, and today the body does it without a word. Today's word bends the knee.
screen: `ONE KNEE IN THE AISLE.` → `A WHOLE CHURCH BOWS.` → `THE BODY, WITHOUT A WORD.`

segments.voice: Genuflect comes from two Latin words: genu, knee, and flectere, to bend. To bend the knee. It's an old sign of honor. At Mass, Catholics do it toward one thing: the tabernacle, the small locked cabinet where the consecrated bread from Mass is kept. Catholics believe that bread is Christ himself, really present. So a lamp, often red, burns near the tabernacle day and night, and the right knee goes down to the floor in front of it, the way you'd greet someone you love and honor. If a church keeps the tabernacle in a side chapel, people bow to the altar instead. Then there's the head. Catholics are asked to bow their heads at the name of Jesus, and at the names of Mary and the saint of the day. And once each Sunday, in the Creed, at the words about Jesus being born of the Virgin Mary and becoming man, everyone is asked to bow. At Christmas and on the feast of the Annunciation, they kneel right down for those words instead. Paul has a line for this, written long before there were church buildings. In the Douay-Rheims: "That in the name of Jesus every knee should bow." People who can't kneel bow instead, and Catholics count that just as much a prayer. Eastern Catholics have their own tradition of deep bows. Catholics would put the point this way: before the words come, before you've had a chance to think, the body has already said what it believes.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bow your head once, meaning it. Settle, and breathe. Sit up straight. Then, slowly, lower your head. Not a nod. A real bow, the kind that takes three seconds going down. Hold it. Notice how it feels to lower yourself on purpose, with nobody watching. If you pray, you can bow toward God. If not, bow toward whatever in your life deserves it: someone's kindness, a gift you didn't earn. Then rise, and sit. The bell holds the time.
Genuflect. To bend the knee, the way Catholics greet Christ present in the tabernacle. Today's word.
Your line: the body says it first. Today, notice what your posture says before you speak: crossed arms, a turned back, a leaning in. Choose one to change. Day ninety-nine.

100.title: The Glory Be
100.hook: the shortest Catholic prayer, praise to the three persons
100.carry: as it was in the beginning
100.tomorrow: The Apostles' Creed, line by line
100.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Glory Be at the end of each decade of the rosary and after the psalms in the Liturgy of the Hours, and many say it on its own at the end of a task or a day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, knees and bows: to genuflect is to bend the knee. Your line was the body says it first. What did your posture say? And today is a milestone. Day one hundred.

Day one hundred. If you've come this far, you've kept at something for over three months, and that deserves a moment. So here's a fitting thing for it: a prayer that takes about seven seconds. It closes each decade of the rosary. It ends the psalms when monks and nuns and priests pray their daily hours. It fits in the gap between one task and the next. It asks for nothing. It doesn't confess anything. It just gives glory, and goes back to work. Today: the Glory Be.
screen: `ONE HUNDRED DAYS.` → `A SEVEN-SECOND PRAYER.` → `IT ASKS FOR NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in its traditional English form: "Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Ghost. As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end. Amen." Many Catholics today say Holy Spirit. In the old Latin: Gloria Patri, et Filio, et Spiritui Sancto. Sicut erat in principio, et nunc, et semper, et in saecula saeculorum. Amen. Today's word is the name for a prayer like this: doxology. From two Greek words: doxa, glory, and logos, word. A glory-word. The Gloria at Mass is called the greater doxology, and this one the lesser. Look at its shape. The first line is the sign of the cross from three days ago, turned from a name into praise: Father, Son, Holy Spirit. The second line is all about time. As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be. Past, present, future, in one breath. And some readers hear a history in that line. Christians once argued fiercely over whether the Son had always existed or had a beginning. Read that way, praying that the glory was the same in the beginning is a way of saying, every day: he always was. A seven-second prayer, carrying an old argument, settled into rhythm. The last phrase, world without end, is the old English way of saying forever: in the Latin, into the ages of ages. Catholics use the Glory Be the way you'd use a period at the end of a sentence. After a psalm. After a decade. After a task. It closes things, and hands them back.
screen: `DOXA AND LOGOS: A GLORY-WORD.` · `FATHER, SON AND HOLY SPIRIT.` · `PAST, PRESENT, FUTURE.` · `AN OLD ARGUMENT IN SEVEN SECONDS.` · then, large: `AS IT WAS IN THE BEGINNING, IS NOW, AND EVER SHALL BE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: close something. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you finished today, or will finish soon. A report, a load of laundry, a hard conversation. When it's done, before you move to the next thing, stop for seven seconds. If you pray, say the Glory Be over it. If you don't, simply mark the end: done, and let it go. For now, just sit with the feeling of something finished. The bell holds the time.
Doxology. A glory-word: a short prayer of praise, like the Glory Be, to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Today's word.
Your line: as it was in the beginning. Today, at the end of one task, pause for seven seconds before starting the next. Day one hundred.

101.title: The Apostles' Creed, line by line
101.hook: twelve lines, from creator to life everlasting
101.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Apostles' Creed at the start of the rosary and at baptisms, and it may replace the longer Nicene Creed at Sunday Mass, especially in Lent and the Easter season.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Glory Be, a doxology, a glory-word. Your line was as it was in the beginning. Did you close a task with seven seconds? Day one hundred and one.

Rome, in the early Church, as an old church order describes it. It's the night before Easter, in the dark. A woman stands waist-deep in water. A church leader asks her a question: do you believe in God, the Father almighty? She says: I believe. And she's plunged under. Do you believe in Christ Jesus, the Son of God? I believe. Under again. Do you believe in the Holy Spirit, and the holy Church? I believe. Under a third time, and up, and she's a Christian. Those questions, asked at the water, slowly grew into a single statement Catholics still say today. Today's word is its name.
screen: `ROME, AN EARLY EASTER NIGHT.` → `THREE QUESTIONS IN THE WATER.` → `I BELIEVE. I BELIEVE. I BELIEVE.`

segments.voice: Creed comes from the Latin credo: I believe. The Apostles' Creed opens in Latin: Credo in Deum, Patrem omnipotentem, Creatorem caeli et terrae. I believe in God, the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth. Then it moves like a story. Jesus Christ, his only Son. Conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary. Suffered under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He descended to the dead, rose on the third day, ascended into heaven, and will come to judge the living and the dead. Then the Holy Spirit, the holy catholic Church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the body, and life everlasting. Notice Pontius Pilate. Besides Jesus and Mary, the one person the creed names is a Roman governor. It pins the whole thing to a real time and place. Now, why the Apostles'? An old legend, written down around the year 400, says the twelve apostles each gave one line before they went out into the world. Historians say it grew more slowly, from those baptism questions in Rome, reaching its present shape centuries later. The Church uses it either way, as a faithful summary of what the apostles taught. And here's the thing to carry. Credo isn't a list of opinions. Some linguists connect it with an ancient root that may mean to put your heart. To believe, in this old sense, isn't to hold a fact in your head. It's to set your heart on something, and lean your weight there. That's something you do.
screen: `CREDO: I BELIEVE.` · `A STORY IN TWELVE LINES.` · `A LEGEND, AND A SLOWER HISTORY.` · `TO PUT YOUR HEART.` · then, large: `CREDO IN DEUM, PATREM OMNIPOTENTEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the creed, slowly. Settle, and breathe. If you know the Apostles' Creed by heart, say it in your mind one line at a time, and after each line, stop and take a breath. Don't rush to the end. If you don't know it, take just the first line: I believe in God, the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth. Say it once, then sit with it. Whether you believe it or not, notice what it would mean to lean your weight there. The bell holds the time.
Creed. From credo, I believe: a short statement of faith, with roots in questions asked at baptism. Today's word.
Your line: I believe is a verb. Today, notice one thing you say you believe in, and do one small thing that leans your weight on it. Day one hundred and one.

102.title: The morning offering
102.hook: offering the whole day, work and joys and trouble, before it starts
102.howItsDone: Many Catholics say a morning offering on waking, often a prayer from the Apostleship of Prayer (now the Pope's Worldwide Prayer Network) that offers the day's prayers, works, joys and sufferings, joined to the Pope's intention for the month.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Apostles' Creed, and the word creed: I believe. Your line was I believe is a verb. Where did you lean your weight? Day one hundred and two.

Your alarm goes off. Before your eyes are fully open, your hand is already reaching for the phone. And in the next ninety seconds, the day gets handed out. To the news. To the group chat. To a work email that makes your stomach drop. To somebody's vacation photos. By the time your feet touch the floor, your day already belongs to a dozen people, and you never decided to give it to any of them. There's an old Catholic habit that gets there first. Before anything else claims the day, you give the whole thing away, on purpose, to God. Today: the morning offering.
screen: `THE ALARM, THE PHONE.` → `THE DAY GETS HANDED OUT.` → `GIVE IT AWAY FIRST.`

segments.voice: In 1844, in a Jesuit house in the south of France, a group of young men training to be priests were restless. They wanted to be missionaries, off in distant countries, doing something that mattered. Instead they were stuck with books and chores. Their spiritual director, a priest named François-Xavier Gautrelet, told them something that changed their mood. You can be missionaries right now, he said, here. Offer everything you do today, the study, the dishes, the boredom, for the work of the Church around the world. That became a movement called the Apostleship of Prayer, and it spread to millions. It lives on today as the Pope's Worldwide Prayer Network. Its heart is a short prayer said on waking. The words vary, but it offers to God, through the heart of Jesus, all the prayers, works, joys and sufferings of the day ahead, often joined to a particular intention the Pope asks people to pray for that month. Notice what's in that list. Not just the good parts. The joys, and the sufferings. The meeting you dread. The kid who won't get dressed. The pain in your back. All of it, handed over before it happens. The idea goes back to Paul. In the Douay-Rheims he asks Christians to "present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing unto God." Not a sacrifice on an altar. A whole ordinary life, offered. So nothing in the day is wasted, even the parts that feel like a waste. Catholics would say the day is already given, so it already counts.
screen: `1844: YOUNG MEN, RESTLESS.` · `BE MISSIONARIES RIGHT HERE.` · `PRAYERS, WORKS, JOYS, SUFFERINGS.` · `NOTHING IN THE DAY IS WASTED.` · then, large: `PRESENT YOUR BODIES A LIVING SACRIFICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse tomorrow morning. Settle, and breathe. Picture waking up tomorrow. The alarm. Your hand moving toward the phone. Now picture stopping it. Hand still. And before anything else gets the day, you give it away first. If you pray, you can offer the whole day to God, work, joys and trouble, in a few words of your own, or with a morning offering from a prayer book. If you don't, simply decide what the day is for. The bell holds the time.
The morning offering. A short prayer on waking that gives the whole day to God before it starts, joys and sufferings too. Today's word.
Your line: today is already given. Tomorrow morning, before you check your phone, give the day away first. Even ten seconds counts. Day one hundred and two.

103.title: The Angelus
103.hook: the noon bell, three verses, three Hail Marys, remembering the angel came
103.howItsDone: Catholics traditionally pray the Angelus at 6 a.m., noon and 6 p.m., often at the ringing of a church bell: three short verses, each followed by a Hail Mary, and a closing prayer; in the Easter season the Regina Caeli is prayed instead, and the Pope leads it from his window every Sunday at noon.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the morning offering, giving the day away before it starts. Your line was today is already given. Did you get there before the phone did? Day one hundred and three.

There's a French painting from the 1850s. Two peasants, a man and a woman, stand in a flat, brown field at the end of the day. A pitchfork is stuck in the ground. A basket of potatoes sits at their feet. Far off on the horizon, there's a tiny church steeple. The man has taken off his hat. The woman's hands are folded and her head is bowed. They've stopped working, right in the middle of the field, because the church bell has just rung. The painter, Jean-François Millet, named the painting after the prayer they're saying. Today: the Angelus.
screen: `TWO PEASANTS IN A FIELD.` → `A DISTANT BELL.` → `THEY STOP, AND PRAY.`

segments.voice: The Angelus takes its name from its first words in Latin: Angelus Domini nuntiavit Mariae. The angel of the Lord declared unto Mary. Traditionally, church bells rang it three times a day: morning, noon and evening. The traditional pattern is three strokes, a pause, three, a pause, three, then nine. The custom was to stop wherever you were: in the field, the kitchen, the market. The prayer walks through the moment the angel Gabriel came to Mary, in three short verses, each followed by a Hail Mary. First: the angel declared unto Mary, and she conceived of the Holy Spirit. Second, Mary's own answer, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word." Third, from the opening of John's Gospel: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." At that line, people traditionally kneel or bow. Then a short closing prayer. That third verse is the whole point. Catholics believe that God, in that moment, took on a human body. In Catholic teaching, the eternal Word came into time and flesh and a small town. So three times a day, in the middle of ordinary work, the Angelus remembers that God came into ordinary life. In the Easter season a different prayer takes its place, the Regina Caeli, Queen of Heaven, rejoice. And every Sunday at noon, the Pope still leads the Angelus from a window over Saint Peter's Square. That also closes this part of the camp, the body praying: the sign of the cross, holy water, the bended knee, the Glory Be, the Creed, the morning offering, and now a bell at noon.
screen: `THE ANGEL OF THE LORD DECLARED.` · `THREE BELLS, THREE VERSES.` · `BE IT DONE TO ME.` · `GOD CAME INTO ORDINARY LIFE.` · then, large: `AND THE WORD WAS MADE FLESH, AND DWELT AMONG US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a bell in the middle of the day. Settle, and breathe. Picture noon today, or tomorrow, wherever you'll be: at a desk, in a car, in line. Now picture stopping there for thirty seconds, the way the two peasants stopped in the field. If you pray, you can say one Hail Mary. It begins, in the Douay-Rheims: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee." If you don't, simply stop, look up from the work, and let the middle of the day be quiet. The bell holds the time.
Angelus. Latin for angel: a prayer at morning, noon and evening, remembering the angel came to Mary, and the Word was made flesh. Today's word.
Your line: the word was made flesh. Set an alarm for noon today. When it rings, stop what you're doing for thirty seconds, wherever you are. Day one hundred and three.

104.title: The entrance
104.hook: the procession, the sign of the cross, and the priest kissing the altar
104.howItsDone: At the start of Mass the congregation stands and sings as the priest and ministers process to the altar; the priest kisses the altar, everyone makes the sign of the cross together, and the priest greets the people, who answer him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Angelus, a bell at noon. Your line was the word was made flesh. Did you stop when the alarm rang? Now a new part: the Mass, scene by scene. Day one hundred and four.

Sunday morning. People drift in: families wrestling toddlers, an old man with a cane, teenagers who clearly got dragged. Some kneel and pray. Some chat in whispers. Some scroll their phones until the last second. Then a bell rings, or the organ starts, and everyone stands. For the next two weeks, we're going to walk through the Catholic Mass one scene at a time, the way you'd walk someone through a play they've never seen. A guest at Mass can feel a step behind: everyone else seems to know when to stand, what to say, where to look. Let's start where the Mass starts. Today: the entrance.
screen: `SUNDAY: PEOPLE DRIFT IN.` → `A BELL, AND EVERYONE STANDS.` → `THE MASS, SCENE BY SCENE.`

segments.voice: First, a procession comes up the aisle while everyone sings. At the front, someone carries a cross on a tall pole. Candles on either side. Sometimes incense, swinging in a metal holder and filling the air with smoke. Then the servers, a reader, and a deacon holding up a large book of the Gospels. The priest walks last. Everyone is walking toward the same thing: the altar. When the priest reaches it, he bows, and then he does something a first-time visitor may not expect. He leans down and kisses it. Why kiss a table? Catholics see the altar as a sign of Christ himself, and it's where the sacrifice of the Mass will be offered. And there's an old reason too. Tradition says early Christians gathered for Mass at the tombs of martyrs, and to this day some altars hold a small relic of a saint. That cloud of witnesses from last week is, quite literally, built into the altar. Then the priest turns to the people, and the whole church makes the sign of the cross together. You learned it a week ago. This is where the Mass begins with it. Then he greets them. In Latin, Dominus vobiscum: the Lord be with you. It's an old greeting. In the book of Ruth, a farmer named Boaz walks into his field and says to the workers, in the Douay-Rheims: "The Lord be with you." They answer back. And that's the point of the entrance. Before anyone prays, before anyone reads, before the bread, the people come together. The Mass isn't something you watch. It's something a gathered crowd does.
screen: `A PROCESSION TO THE ALTAR.` · `THE PRIEST KISSES THE ALTAR.` · `THE SIGN OF THE CROSS, TOGETHER.` · `THE LORD BE WITH YOU.` · then: `A GATHERED CROWD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: arrive early and still. Settle, and breathe. Think of the next place you're going today: work, a class, a dinner, a meeting. Picture getting there five minutes early. Not to answer emails in the parking lot. Just to arrive. To notice the room, the people coming in, the light. If you pray, you can ask God to be with the people you'll meet there. If you don't, just be the one who got there first, and let it settle. The bell holds the time.
The entrance. The Mass begins with a procession, a kissed altar, the sign of the cross and a greeting. The crowd gathers first. Today's word.
Your line: we gather first. Today, arrive somewhere five minutes early, and spend them being there, not getting ready to leave. Day one hundred and four.

105.title: Through my fault
105.hook: the whole church admits it has sinned and asks each other for prayer
105.howItsDone: At the start of most Masses, after a brief silence, priest and people pray the Confiteor together, many striking their breast at 'through my fault'; it is one of several forms of the penitential act and does not replace the sacrament of confession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the entrance: a procession, a kissed altar, a greeting. Your line was we gather first. Did you arrive early anywhere? Day one hundred and five.

A staff meeting begins. Everyone stands up, the boss included, and says out loud, together: I've messed up. In what I thought, what I said, what I did, and what I didn't do. It's my fault. Then everyone turns to the people around them and says: please pray for me. It would be the strangest meeting of the year. And it's roughly what can happen in the first minutes of a Catholic Mass. Right after the greeting, before a single reading, the whole church owns up. Today's word is the prayer they say.
screen: `A MEETING THAT STARTS WITH SORRY.` → `EVERYONE, THE BOSS INCLUDED.` → `THE FIRST MINUTES OF MASS.`

segments.voice: It's called the Confiteor, from its first word in Latin: I confess. The priest invites everyone to call their sins to mind, and there's a short silence. Then priest and people together say they confess to almighty God, and to each other, that they have greatly sinned, in their thoughts and in their words, in what they have done and in what they have failed to do. That last part is sharp. Not just the wrong things. The good things left undone. Then comes the line, in the old Latin: mea culpa, mea culpa, mea maxima culpa. Through my fault, through my fault, through my most grievous fault. And as they say it, people strike their chest with a closed hand. That gesture echoes a story Jesus told. A tax collector stands at the back of the Temple, won't even lift his eyes, beats his breast and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "O God, be merciful to me a sinner." Jesus says that man went home right with God. Then the Confiteor turns outward. Everyone asks Mary, the angels and the saints, and you, my brothers and sisters, to pray for me. You confess to the people beside you, and then you ask them for help. Nobody stands above anybody. The priest says it too. The Church is clear that this isn't the sacrament of confession. It doesn't replace that. It's a way of starting honestly. Looking back over this week, from bending the knee to the Angelus to the entrance, the body keeps saying things before words do. Here, it's a fist on the chest.
screen: `CONFITEOR: I CONFESS.` · `DONE, AND FAILED TO DO.` · `MEA CULPA, AND A FIST ON THE CHEST.` · `PRAY FOR ME, BROTHERS AND SISTERS.` · then, large: `O GOD, BE MERCIFUL TO ME A SINNER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one honest moment. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last day or two. Not to punish yourself. Just to see clearly. One thing you did that you wish you hadn't. One thing you left undone. If you're Catholic, or you'd like to, you can strike your chest gently, once, the way the tax collector did. If you pray, you can use his words. If not, just name it, and set it down. The bell holds the time.
Confiteor. I confess: the prayer at the start of Mass where everyone admits their sins and asks each other for prayer. Today's word.
Your line: we all begin as sinners. Today, when you're tempted to feel above someone, remember a whole church starting Mass by saying my fault. Day one hundred and five.

fork.setup: you're the tax collector at the back of the Temple. you can't even lift your eyes. what do you do?
options: list your good deeds to balance things out.
beat your breast and ask God for mercy.
leave before anyone notices you.
fork.reveal: he beat his breast and said: "O God, be merciful to me a sinner." Jesus says he went home right with God. the fist on the chest at Mass echoes him.

original.script: mea culpa, mea culpa, mea maxima culpa
original.note: Latin: through my fault, through my fault, through my most grievous fault.

trapdoor: what you thought: mea culpa, a fancy way to say oops.
what it means: a whole church owning its sins together, then asking each other for prayer.
what a scholar hears: confiteor, I confess; cogitatione, verbo, opere et omissione, in thought, word, deed and omission. and a fist on the chest from Luke 18.
